Chapter 23 · Diversification and today · 1947–hoy

Ethics, controversies and open science

From the Nuremberg Code to the replication crisis: how psychology learned to protect people and to check its own results.

A science that studies people has two responsibilities: not to harm those who take part and not to mislead those who read its results. Psychology has had to learn both lessons, sometimes from serious mistakes. This chapter tells how.

What were people trying to understand?

What limits experiments on people and animals must respect, what to do when a researcher fabricates data and why some published results are not confirmed when other teams repeat the study.

With what methods?

Ethics codes, review committees and, more recently, large-scale replication studies. After the trials of the Nazi doctors, the Nuremberg Code (1947) established that the voluntary consent of the participant is essential. The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) developed it for medical research. In the United States, the scandal of the Tuskegee study, in which hundreds of African American men were left with untreated syphilis for forty years, led to the Belmont Report (1979), with three principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

Who took part?

In psychology, Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments and other studies involving deception and stress opened an intense debate about participants' welfare. The APA approved its first code of ethics in 1953, and since the 1970s almost all research with people has gone through an ethics committee. In Spain the psychologists' Code of Ethics was approved in 1987.

The second lesson came in 2011. That year it emerged that the Dutch social psychologist Diederik Stapel had invented the data for dozens of articles. In the same year Daryl Bem published in a prestigious journal experiments that seemed to demonstrate precognition, using statistical methods common in the discipline. If those methods could "prove" something so improbable, the problem lay in the methods. In 2015 a project coordinated by Brian Nosek repeated 100 studies published in major journals: only about 36% obtained significant results like the original.

What did it contribute?

  • Informed consent, the right to withdraw and confidentiality as basic rules.
  • Preregistration: announcing a study's plan before collecting the data.
  • Registered reports, which journals accept before the results are known.
  • Open publication of data, materials and code, and replications across many laboratories.

What was revised later?

The replication crisis also affected medicine, economics and other sciences, and psychology has been one of the disciplines that has done most to tackle it. Not every study that fails to replicate was false: some depended on specific conditions. But widely publicised effects such as "ego depletion" and some forms of social priming have been called into question. On the ethical side, the Hoffman report (2015) revealed that members of the APA had collaborated with abusive interrogations after 9/11, which led the association to change its code. The general lesson is that science is not infallible, but it can correct itself if it is given the means.

When you read a news story about a psychology study, it is worth asking how many people took part, whether it has been replicated and whether the effect is large or merely "statistically significant".

References

  1. National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects (1979). The Belmont Report. Washington: US Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.
  2. Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716.
  3. Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D. y Simonsohn, U. (2011). False-positive psychology. Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359–1366.
  4. Nosek, B. A., Ebersole, C. R., DeHaven, A. C. y Mellor, D. T. (2018). The preregistration revolution. PNAS, 115(11), 2600–2606.
  5. Consejo General de la Psicología de España (2010). Código Deontológico del Psicólogo (versión revisada). Madrid.
